literal: Changsun Fei; Wei Guzhen
idiomatic: Biographies of Changsun Fei and Wei Guzhen

literal: Changsun Fei was a man of Dai.
idiomatic: Changsun Fei came from Dai.

literal: In Emperor Zhaocheng's reign, at age thirteen he was chosen as inner attendant.
idiomatic: At thirteen, in the reign of Emperor Zhaocheng, he was selected to serve within the palace.

literal: In youth he had refined bearing; resolute and sparing of speech.
idiomatic: Even young he carried himself with quiet dignity—decisive, steady, and not given to many words.

literal: When Taizu was among the Dugu and Helan tribes, Fei constantly attended him, warding off insult at his side; Taizu deeply trusted and relied on him.
idiomatic: While Taizu still lived among the Dugu and the Helan, Fei stayed at his side day and night, shielding him from affront; Taizu came to trust him as one trusts a weapon in the hand.

literal: At the opening of Dengguo, with Mo Ti and others he was made great general; he followed the campaign against Liu Xian, from Ruyuan struck the Kumo Xi, and subdued the Helan tribe—all with battle merit.
idiomatic: When the Dengguo era began he stood among the great generals with Mo Ti and the rest: he marched against Liu Xian, struck the Kumo Xi from Ruyuan, and brought down the Helan—each campaign adding to his name.

literal: Taizu campaigned against the Rouran and broke them utterly; Fei received the surrender of their lord Pihouba—the affair is set forth in the Rouran annals.
idiomatic: On Taizu's campaign against the Rouran, which shattered them utterly, Fei took the surrender of their lord Pihouba; the full account is in the Rouran biography.

literal: He also followed the campaigns against Wei Chen and the Xuegan tribe and destroyed them.
idiomatic: He marched again against Wei Chen and the Xuegan and wiped them out.

literal: A Rouran splinter lord, Wenheti's son Heduo Han and others, led their clans in abandoning their father and fleeing west; Fei with light cavalry pursued to Shangjun and beheaded him.
idiomatic: When Wenheti's son Heduo Han and other splinter chiefs dragged their clans westward, deserting their father, Fei overtook them at Shangjun with a flying column and took Heduo Han's head.

literal: Later he followed the campaign against Zhongshan and was appointed Central Army Commander-General.
idiomatic: He later joined the siege of Zhongshan and was named Central Army Commander-General.

literal: The imperial carriage halted at Jinyang; Murong Bao's inspector of Bingzhou and Prince of Liaoxi Nong abandoned the city and fled by night; Fei pursued to Puquan and seized his wife and children.
idiomatic: When the court paused at Jinyang, Murong Bao's Bingzhou inspector and Prince of Liaoxi, Nong, slipped from the walls under cover of dark; Fei ran him down to Puquan and took wife and children.

literal: Taizu was about to invest Zhongshan; Murong Bao abandoned the city and fled to Helong.
idiomatic: As Taizu closed in on Zhongshan, Murong Bao fled the city for Helong.

literal: Fei with the Left General Li Li and three thousand horse pursued to Fanyang, did not overtake them, and returned.
idiomatic: Fei and the Left General Li Li rode three thousand after him as far as Fanyang; they could not catch him and turned back.

literal: He then broke the Yancheng garrison and took more than a thousand captives.
idiomatic: He then stormed the Yancheng garrison and carried off more than a thousand prisoners.

literal: Within Zhongshan the people set up Murong Pulin as lord; Taizu invested the city.
idiomatic: The folk inside Zhongshan raised Murong Pulin as their leader while Taizu tightened the ring about the walls.

literal: Pulin then sent out more than a thousand foot soldiers, intending to watch for an opening and strike the encirclement.
idiomatic: Pulin sent out a thousand foot soldiers, hoping to catch the siege at a weak moment and break through.

literal: Taizu ordered Fei to offer challenge and feign retreat; Pulin's host pursued Fei, and Taizu cut their rear—all were seized and beheaded.
idiomatic: Taizu had Fei offer battle and then feign flight; when Pulin's men rushed after Fei, Taizu closed on their rear and took every man—none left alive.

literal: At the time, with few troops and horses and short of grain, they lifted the siege of Zhongshan and drew provisions from Hejian.
idiomatic: Supplies and horses were thin; the siege of Zhongshan was raised, and the army fed itself from Hejian.

literal: Murong Helin killed Pulin and set himself up as lord.
idiomatic: Murong Helin slew Pulin and declared himself ruler.

literal: The imperial carriage halted at Lukou and sent Fei at the head of seven thousand horse to strike Zhongshan; he entered the outer wards and returned.
idiomatic: The court camped at Lukou and sent Fei with seven thousand riders to raid Zhongshan; he broke into the outer city and withdrew.

literal: Helin with four thousand foot and horse pursued Fei to the Bosi River; Fei from Weichang struck them and took two hundred armored riders.
idiomatic: Helin came after him with four thousand foot and horse as far as the Bosi River; Fei wheeled from Weichang, struck, and seized two hundred armored riders.

literal: Fei was struck by a stray arrow; the wound was grave, and he returned.
idiomatic: A shaft found Fei; the wound was deep, and he had to turn back.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified, for merit he was enfeoffed Duke of Langye.
idiomatic: After Zhongshan fell, his service won him the ducal title of Langye.

literal: He was transferred to Commandant of the Guard and his enfeoffment changed to Luxiang.
idiomatic: He was moved to Commandant of the Guard, and his fief was changed to Luxiang.

literal: At that time the Zhongshan prefect Qiu Ru was unwilling to move inward; he hid himself in Zhao commandery and set up the bandit chief Zhao Zhun as leader.
idiomatic: The Zhongshan prefect Qiu Ru, loath to be resettled inland, vanished into Zhao commandery and made the outlaw Zhao Zhun his figurehead.

literal: He falsely forged demonic words, saying: "Yan tilts eastward; Zhao shall continue. To know the name—Huai waters are not enough."
idiomatic: He invented a sorcerer's prophecy: "The Yan realm leans east; Zhao will rise in its place. Would you know the name? The Huai cannot hold it all."

literal: Zhun rejoiced and followed him; he styled himself Bearer of the Staff, Grand General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Qing and Ji provinces, Duke of Julu—Ru as chief clerk; they gathered a party of more than two thousand, held Guancheng, linked with the Dingling, killed chief officials, and stirred Changshan, Julu, and Guangping commanderies.
idiomatic: Zhun took the bait and followed; he called himself Bearer of the Staff, Grand General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Qing and Ji, Duke of Julu, with Ru as chief clerk. More than two thousand men rallied at Guancheng, the Dingling were drawn in, magistrates were cut down, and rebellion spread through Changshan, Julu, and Guangping.

literal: Fei was sent at the head of three thousand horse to suppress them; he broke Zhun at Jiumen, beheaded Qiu Ru, and took Zhun alive.
idiomatic: Fei was dispatched with three thousand horse, shattered Zhun at Jiumen, struck off Qiu Ru's head, and brought Zhun in bonds.

literal: An edict made Ru's flesh food; Zhun was sent to the capital, drawn and quartered in the market, and his clan exterminated.
idiomatic: By edict Ru's flesh was made a public feast; Zhun was sent to the capital, torn apart in the market, and his house rooted out to the last man.

literal: Fei was appointed Pacification of Distant Regions General and inspector of Yanzhou, given twenty thousand foot and horse; he marched south on Xuchang and carried the frontier to Pengcheng.
idiomatic: Fei was named Pacification of Distant Regions General and inspector of Yanzhou, given twenty thousand foot and horse; he drove south against Xuchang and pushed the border to Pengcheng.

literal: Sima Dezong's general Liu Gai sent envoys to Fei to surrender and presented the products of his region.
idiomatic: Liu Gai, a Jin general under Sima Dezong, sent envoys to offer surrender to Fei and sent tribute from his district.

literal: Yao Ping raided Pingyang; Taizu was about to campaign against him and, choosing among the generals, found none to surpass Fei; he summoned Fei back to the capital and sent Fei with the Prince of Piling Shun and others—sixty thousand horse—as vanguard.
idiomatic: When Yao Ping struck at Pingyang, Taizu prepared to march against him; among all his captains none outranked Fei, so Fei was recalled to the capital and sent ahead with Prince of Piling Shun and the rest—sixty thousand horse in the van.

literal: The imperial carriage halted at Yong'an; Ping recruited brave officers who led two hundred picked horse to spy on the army; Fei met them in counterattack and seized them—not a single horse returned.
idiomatic: The court paused at Yong'an; Ping sent daring officers with two hundred elite riders to probe the host; Fei met them head-on and took every man—not one horse rode back.

literal: Ping withdrew to hold Chaibi; Taizu advanced, attacked, and slaughtered the place.
idiomatic: Ping fell back to Chaibi; Taizu pressed the siege and took the city by storm.

literal: Fei was sent back to garrison Yanzhou.
idiomatic: Fei was returned to his post at Yanzhou.

literal: Fei comforted the people south of the Yellow River, winning the hearts of officials and commoners; his authority and trust stood out along the Huai and Si.
idiomatic: South of the river he soothed the land and won officials and people alike; along the Huai and the Si his name was law.

literal: Skilled in stratagem, foremost in courage among the generals, in every battle he commonly went before the soldiers as their vanguard; in campaigns before and after he never knew defeat—hence whenever great peril arose, they set Fei to face it.
idiomatic: Clever in counsel and first in valor among the captains, he habitually led from the front; campaign after campaign he never tasted defeat—so whenever disaster loomed, it was Fei they sent to meet it.

literal: In pacifying the central plains southward and crushing Qiang raiders westward, Fei's merit was greatest; he was rewarded with several hundred household slaves and livestock counted by the thousand.
idiomatic: Of the work that subdued the central plains and broke the Qiang in the west, Fei's share was the largest; reward came in hundreds of bondsmen and herds numbered in thousands.

literal: Later his noble rank was reduced to Marquis of Lantian.
idiomatic: Later his title was lowered to Marquis of Lantian.

literal: In the fifth year of Tianci he died; posthumous name Wu; buried with honor at Jinling.
idiomatic: He died in the fifth year of Tianci, was given the posthumous name Wu, and was laid to rest with honor beside Jinling.

literal: His son Han inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Han succeeded to the fief.

literal: Han in youth had his father's manner.
idiomatic: In youth Han bore his father's stamp.

literal: In Taizu's time, for skill in mounted archery he was made hunting attendant.
idiomatic: Under Taizu his riding and bow won him a place as hunting attendant.

literal: When Taizong was still abroad, Han with Yuan Mohun and others secretly plotted to welcome and install him.
idiomatic: While Taizong was still in exile, Han joined Yuan Mohun and others in a secret plan to bring him to the throne.

literal: When Taizong took the throne, Han was transferred to attendant-in-ordinary; with Mohun and others he attended to remonstrance at the emperor's side.
idiomatic: At Taizong's accession Han became attendant-in-ordinary; he and Mohun and the rest kept watch at the emperor's ear.

literal: For merit he was transferred to Pacify-the-South General.
idiomatic: Merit raised him to Pacify-the-South General.

literal: He led forces to garrison the northern frontier; his renown was very great, and the Rouran feared him.
idiomatic: He took command on the northern marches; his name alone made the Rouran uneasy.

literal: Later he was made overseer of all military affairs in the north, Pacify-the-North General, and Marquis of Zhending; he was given the palace's fine picket company and the honor of banners, drums, and pipes.
idiomatic: He was later named overseer of northern armies, Pacify-the-North General, and Marquis of Zhending, with the palace's elite picket and the full panoply of banners, drums, and pipes.

literal: Whenever the Rouran raided the frontier, Han repelled them with merit and was advanced in rank to duke.
idiomatic: Each Rouran raid on the border met Han's counterstroke and added to his honors until he was raised to duke.

literal: When Shizu took the throne, Han was summoned back to the capital, advanced to Prince of Pingyang, and given the additional title Pacification General.
idiomatic: At Shizu's accession Han was recalled to the capital, made Prince of Pingyang, and given the added title Pacification General.

literal: When the Rouran Datán raided Yunzhong, Shizu campaigned in person and sent Han at the head of the northern generals Wei Juan; from north of Canhe they struck Datán's splinter chief Afugan at Zuo Mountain, beheading several thousand and taking more than ten thousand horses.
idiomatic: When Datán of the Rouran struck Yunzhong, Shizu marched in person and sent Han with the northern commanders, including Wei Juan; north of Canhe they fell on Datán's lieutenant Afugan at Zuo Mountain, taking thousands of heads and more than ten thousand horses.

literal: He also with the Eastern Peace Duke E Qing went out along the Chang River to campaign against Datán.
idiomatic: He also marched along the Chang River with the Eastern Peace Duke, E Qing, to hunt Datán.

literal: Datán's host fled north; they pursued, seized the booty, and returned.
idiomatic: Datán's army ran north; the pursuers gathered the spoils and came home.

literal: Soon he was transferred to Minister over the Masses.
idiomatic: He was soon moved to Minister over the Masses.

literal: He attacked Helian Chang and broke him.
idiomatic: He struck Helian Chang and shattered him.

literal: Shizu again campaigned against Chang; Han with the Director of Justice Daosheng and the Director of the Imperial Clan E Qing led thirty thousand horse as vanguard.
idiomatic: When Shizu marched on Chang again, Han with Daosheng the Director of Justice and E Qing the Director of the Imperial Clan rode thirty thousand ahead of the host.

literal: Chang was defeated and fled to Shanggui; Han with eight thousand horse pursued to Gaoping, did not overtake him, and returned.
idiomatic: Chang broke and ran for Shanggui; Han with eight thousand chased as far as Gaoping, failed to catch him, and turned back.

literal: He followed the strike against the Rouran; the imperial carriage crossed the desert, and Datán fled.
idiomatic: He joined the campaign against the Rouran; the court crossed the desert and Datán fled before them.

literal: His younger brother Pili led forces to join him; meeting Han in battle, Pili's host collapsed and fled; several hundred of their chieftains were beheaded.
idiomatic: Datán's brother Pili came up with an army; Han met him in battle, broke the host, and struck off the heads of several hundred chieftains.

literal: Han was upright, pure, and sternly clear; skilled in comforting generals and soldiers; Taizu greatly valued him.
idiomatic: Upright, incorruptible, and severe in judgment, yet gentle with his officers and men, Han stood high in Taizu's esteem.

literal: In the third year of Shenju he died; the court mourned him deeply, wept for him, attended his funeral in person, and the rites followed the precedent of Prince of Ancheng Shusun Jun, with added funeral gifts.
idiomatic: He died in the third year of Shenju; the throne grieved openly, wept at his bier, came in person to the mourning hall, and ordered rites after the precedent of Prince of Ancheng Shusun Jun, with gifts beyond the usual measure.

literal: Posthumous name Wei; buried with honor at Jinling.
idiomatic: He was given the posthumous name Wei and buried with honor beside Jinling.

literal: His son Pingcheng inherited the enfeoffment and was reduced to duke.
idiomatic: His son Pingcheng succeeded to the fief, which was lowered to a ducal house.

literal: Pingcheng in youth, through his father's position, was made palace attendant; he rose in succession to southern minister.
idiomatic: Young Pingcheng entered service through his father's rank as palace attendant and climbed to southern minister.

literal: He died and was buried with honor at Jinling.
idiomatic: He died and was laid to rest with honor at Jinling.

literal: His son Hun inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Hun took up the fief.

literal: Hun at first was palace attendant; after a long while he became garrison commandant of Pengcheng.
idiomatic: Hun began as palace attendant; in time he was made garrison commandant of Pengcheng.

literal: In the Taihe era he died.
idiomatic: He died during the Taihe reign.

literal: His son Sheng inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Sheng inherited the title.

literal: Han's younger brother Shouxing.
idiomatic: Han had a younger brother, Shouxing.

literal: In Shizu's time he followed the campaign against Pingliang; for merit he was enfeoffed Marquis of Changjin and appointed governor of Hejian.
idiomatic: Under Shizu he marched on Pingliang; merit made him Marquis of Changjin and governor of Hejian.

literal: He perished.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Andu inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Andu succeeded to the fief.

literal: In Xianzu's time he was director of the imperial stud.
idiomatic: Under Xianzu he directed the imperial stud.

literal: His son Tou inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Tou inherited the title.

literal: In Gaozong's time he was palace attendant, then transferred to director of the inner palace and overseer of the dragon-herd office.
idiomatic: Under Gaozong he served as palace attendant, then as director of the inner palace and overseer of the dragon-herd herds.

literal: At the opening of Tian'an he died.
idiomatic: He died at the beginning of the Tian'an era.

literal: His son Ba inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Ba took up the fief.

literal: Chen, younger brother of Lan.
idiomatic: Chen was the younger brother of Lan.

literal: At the opening of Shizu's reign he was palace attendant.
idiomatic: When Shizu first took power he entered the palace as attendant.

literal: He constantly followed campaigns, oversaw imperial weapons, and received very rich rewards.
idiomatic: He rode on campaign after campaign, kept charge of the imperial armory, and was rewarded again and again.

literal: Later, for merit in breaking Pingliang, he was enfeoffed Marquis of Suiyang and given the additional title Inspiring Martial Might General.
idiomatic: Merit at the fall of Pingliang won him Marquis of Suiyang and the added rank Inspiring Martial Might General.

literal: He was transferred to attendant-in-ordinary and northern minister.
idiomatic: He rose to attendant-in-ordinary and northern minister.

literal: Later he was appointed inspector of Yuzhou.
idiomatic: He was later named inspector of Yuzhou.

literal: He expired.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Wugu inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Wugu inherited the fief.

literal: At the opening of Gaozu's reign he went out as garrison commandant of Wudu and entered the court as casual attendant.
idiomatic: When Gaozu began his reign he was posted to Wudu as garrison commandant, then recalled to serve as casual attendant at court.

literal: His son Yue, in Xiaojing's time, was Grand Master of Splendorous Golden Light.
idiomatic: His son Yue, under Emperor Xiaojing, held the rank Grand Master of Splendorous Golden Light.

literal: Fei's younger brother Yigan; at the opening of Taizu's reign he was guardsman of the Feathered Forest.
idiomatic: Fei had a younger brother, Yigan, who at the founding of Taizu's rule served in the Feathered Forest guard.

literal: He followed the pacification of the central plains and was appointed governor of Guangping.
idiomatic: He marched in the conquest of the central plains and was made governor of Guangping.

literal: He met his end.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Shiluo; at the opening of Shizu's reign he was guardsman of the Feathered Forest and gradually rose to attendant-in-ordinary.
idiomatic: His son Shiluo entered the Feathered Forest under Shizu and in time became attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: He followed the campaign against Helian Chang as commander of the van; for merit he was appointed Minister of Music, enfeoffed Duke of Linhuai, and given the additional title Pacify-the-West General.
idiomatic: He fought Helian Chang as a front commander; merit made him Minister of Music, Duke of Linhuai, and Pacify-the-West General.

literal: In Shenju he died; posthumous name Jian.
idiomatic: He died in the Shenju era and was posthumously named Jian.

literal: His son Zhen in youth, through his father's position, was made palace attendant.
idiomatic: His son Zhen, young, entered through his father's rank as palace attendant.

literal: He followed the campaign against Pingliang; for merit he was enfeoffed Marquis of Lincheng and appointed supernumerary attendant-in-ordinary and Broad Martial General.
idiomatic: On the Pingliang campaign merit won him Marquis of Lincheng, supernumerary attendant-in-ordinary, and Broad Martial General.

literal: He inherited his father's enfeoffment, reduced to Establish Righteousness General and Marquis of Linhuai.
idiomatic: He succeeded to his father's title, lowered to Establish Righteousness General and Marquis of Linhuai.

literal: He was transferred to director of the palace guard.
idiomatic: He was moved to director of the palace guard.

literal: He campaigned against Gai Wu.
idiomatic: He marched against Gai Wu.

literal: He was transferred to Director of the Palace Secretariat and given the additional title attendant-in-ordinary.
idiomatic: He was raised to Director of the Palace Secretariat with the added rank of attendant-in-ordinary.
